en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Seventh Chapter
Regarding the Discourse on Giving: Is mental dhamma giving? Yes.
Is it possible to give a mental state to others?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is it possible to give a mental state to others?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is it possible for contact to be given by others?
You should not say so …pe…
Feeling can be attained … perception … volition … [and so on] … consciousness can be attained.
Faith … energy … mindfulness …
“Can concentration … wisdom be given to others?
“One should not say so” … [and so on].
Is it not to be said that "a mental state is giving"?
Yes, it is.
“Is giving a gift of undesirable fruit, of unpleasant fruit, of disagreeable fruit, of fruit that causes one to weep, having suffering as its source and suffering as its result?
“One should not say so.

… [as before] … “Is it not the case that giving is of desirable fruit, of pleasant fruit, of agreeable fruit, of fruit that does not cause one to weep, having happiness as its source and happiness as its result?”
“Yes.
“If giving has a desirable fruit, a pleasant fruit, a agreeable fruit, a fruit that is not to be scorned, and results in happiness and has a happy ripening, then indeed, sir, it should be said:
‘Giving is a mental state.’”
The Blessed One has stated that giving has a desirable fruit; is a gift of robes such? Yes.
Is a gift of robes one that has a desirable fruit, a pleasant fruit, a gratifying fruit, an unsurpassed fruit, a happiness-yielding result, and a happiness-resulting outcome?
It should not be said thus ... [as before] ...
Has it not been stated by the Blessed One that giving has a desirable fruit—that almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick are gifts?
Yes.
“Is the requisite of medicinal supplies for the sick a result that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, gratifying, having happiness as its outcome, and resulting in happiness?
“One should not say so… [as before]… One should not say so.”
“Is a mental state (cetasika dhamma) giving?
Yes. Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Faith, moral shame, and wholesome generosity—
these qualities are followed by the virtuous;
for this, they say, is the divine path.”
"For by this one goes to the world of the gods.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, is it not the case that a mental state is giving?
One should not say:
"A mental state is giving."
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, these five gifts are great gifts, foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient’?”
These things have not been practiced, nor were they practiced in the past; they are not being practiced, nor will they be practiced; they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
What are these five?
Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life.
“Bhikkhus, an Ariyan disciple who abstains from taking life gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings; he gives freedom from enmity;

he gives freedom from affliction. Having given fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction to immeasurable beings, he partakes of immeasurable fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction.”

This, monks, is the first gift, a great gift, primeval, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned taking what is not given...
having abandoned sexual misconduct... [and so forth].
Having abandoned false speech...

[and so on] ...having abandoned the basis for negligence that consists in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, he abstains from the basis for negligence that consists in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.

A noble disciple who abstains from the basis for negligence that consists in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, monks, gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings; he gives freedom from enmity; he gives freedom from affliction.

Having given fearlessness to immeasurable beings, having given freedom from enmity, having given freedom from affliction, one becomes a partaker of immeasurable fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction.

This, monks, is the fifth gift—a great gift, primal, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
These, monks, are the five gifts, the great gifts, which are primal, long-standing, traditional, and ancient.
“Untrodden, not previously trodden upon, not being trodden upon now, nor to be trodden upon in the future,
and unreproached by wise recluses and brahmins”—
is there such a sutta?
“Yes,” [you say].
“In that case, it must not be said that a mental state (cetasika-dhamma) is giving.”
“Is ‘that which is to be given’ (deyyadhamma) the gift (dāna)?
— Yes.
But was it not said by the Blessed One: [as follows]?
“Here someone gives food, gives drink, gives clothing, gives a vehicle, gives a garland, gives perfume, gives unguent, gives a bed, gives a dwelling, gives a lamp.
Is there such a sutta? Yes.
"Therefore, the object to be given is a gift.
"Is the object to be given a gift?
"Yes."
Is it to be said that a gift of merit has a desirable fruit, a pleasant fruit, a gratifying fruit, an intoxicating fruit, a result of happiness, and a ripening of happiness?
No, it should not be so stated... [etc.
...Has it been stated by the Blessed One that giving has a desirable fruit? Has it been stated that the gift of robes has a desirable fruit?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is a robe a desirable fruit, a pleasant fruit, a gratifying fruit, a non-repulsive fruit, having happiness as its outcome, and having happiness as its result?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Has it not been stated by the Blessed One that giving has a desirable fruit— that almsfood is a gift,
lodging is a gift,
and medicinal requisites for the sick are a gift?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is the requisite of medicinal supplies for the sick a result that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and refreshing; one whose outcome is happiness and whose maturation is happiness?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Therefore, it should not be said that "the object to be given is the gift.
The Discussion on Giving is finished.
